contributions.item_title_en: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
contributions.text_english:
There are lessons for Government and political parties from the supplementary budget vote. In a Senedd with no overall majority, co-operation and responsible decision making are essential as we look forward to future budgets. The Government wants to engage constructively across the Senedd to ensure that budgets are a blend, as I see it, of three component parts: funding for the delivery of effective public services, funding for priorities brought into Government by Plaid Cymru, and funding for other priorities from other political parties.

In order to produce a blended budget that can command a Senedd majority, my only plea across the Chamber is that we have a common understanding also of the financial envelope available to us. We are facing the most challenging budget settlement of this decade in 2027-28, with a real-terms reduction of around 0.7 per cent in resource funding, and even greater reductions in capital budgets. The financial envelope for next year's budget is especially tight, and will require a particular discipline for this Government and for all of us who want to play a constructive part in passing Wales's annual budget.

contributions.item_title_en: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
contributions.text_english:
I'm not sure whether I will always welcome a question from Andrew R.T. Davies as Cabinet Minister for Finance, but today in particular, it was particularly useful for me to see that your question, constructed in this manner, allowed me to outline some of my thoughts on how I see the future of budget discussions. And, yes, we are keen, as the First Minister has said, to have discussions with all political parties. We are very conscious of the fact that we are a minority Government. If that supplementary budget vote was useful in anything, it was useful in reminding us, as a Government, that we need to command a majority to pass any budget in this place.

So, I look to all Members here to consider our roles in a different way perhaps to how we have considered our roles and participation in budgets of the past. In fact, the Welsh Conservatives have an advantage over all other political parties here. You're almost the continuity party in this Senedd, because you are an opposition party and you've played—[Interruption.] You're consistently an opposition party; I do not prejudge the future. But Reform is a new party in this Senedd, Labour is a party in opposition for the first time and Plaid Cymru is a party in Government, and there are new roles for all of us to play in that. But I hope that as we continue discussions over the next few weeks and months—. And those discussions are happening, and I want now to use pace and to think about how we can have those discussions across political parties and individuals in this Chamber to bring ideas into this big melting pot that is the annual budget. So, I hope that we can do that in a more meaningful way than we have done coming out of the election before the summer. And I think that's a challenge that all of us have to rise to, and me, in particular, as the finance Minister.

contributions.item_title_en: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
contributions.text_english: Yes, I certainly agree that, in looking at budgets, we need not just to look at those spending lines as they are drafted on a spreadsheet, but we need to look properly at where our outcomes can be improved, and you've listed some of the areas where we need, as Wales, to be doing better, and, certainly, as a Government, we're committed to doing so. So, looking at outcomes, effectiveness and value for money all go hand in hand as we seek, as a new Government in place, in advance of making our own budget and putting it together, as we are looking at efficiencies within Government and outcomes of where we want to prioritise our funding. That piece of work is being undertaken as a budgetary process, but especially in light of our appointment of a Minister with exact responsibility for effectiveness and outcomes of Government action. And that lasting change, of course, that you spoke of, does require something that is more agile and meaningful than annual budgets—so, a commitment to looking to a multi-year budget, but, of course, within the spending review of the allocations to us as a Government. Looking to a multi-year budget is something that I'm looking to propose as part of our budget processes here.

Well, it's always been something that's been a topic of debate in this Senedd, and within Plaid Cymru too, in terms of what is that point where you're striking the balance in the housing market between the housing stock available for people to live in and also the housing stock available for the tourism and self-catering sector, and striking that balance, so that one doesn't have a negative impact on the other, getting that balance right, is important. And that is what we hope to deliver through consulting on this.

I've already had discussions with representatives of the self-catering sector, who, clearly, do believe that the balance is at a lower point than the 152 days in the consultation, and you perhaps feel the same. Now, I am open to having that discussion. I sense that the response to the consultation will demonstrate that the sector itself, and those within the sector, do believe that we need to go deeper than what's contained within the consultation, but the Government does want to strike the right balance. But I am eager that we reach a position where this system that impacts our housing sector, but also our self-catering and tourism sectors, reaches a point where it can be a permanent solution in this area. So, I'm open to discuss this with you too in terms of how we get the outcome to this consultation to reach a point that has majority support in this place.

contributions.item_title_en: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Finance
contributions.text_english: A year-round tourism economy is something that I definitely want to see, both for the constituency that we both represent, but also for Wales generally. I think we've seen significant progress on that over the last few years, but there is more to do still on that. We have our investment priorities, and looking at how we can attract tourists for an extended period of the year is part of the criteria in how we invest in that. Also, we need to make sure that the business rates system that we have, and other taxation aspects, are also ensuring that those businesses that support the hospitality sector are able to be all year round. There's no point having businesses that are only open for a particular part of the year. We need businesses that are open all year long, so that they can provide the opportunity for tourists to benefit, but also, what benefits tourists also benefits the communities they serve. So, I'm particularly hopeful that the positive sign that the Government was able to give yesterday for such a wide array of businesses that do support the tourism sector, of a 30 per cent reduction in business rates from next April, is a positive sign for the tourism sector generally that this Government backs it.

contributions.text_english: There are two aspects to this; I've spoken, actually, twice on the politics show on both of them. The pressures in particular from within the NHS are considerable, and they were considerably more than I expected them to be. They are a challenge within the financial year that I'm trying to manage as we speak. So, those were two aspects that were particularly challenging for public services in Wales.

contributions.item_title_en: 4. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Finance: Rebalancing the non-domestic rates system
contributions.text_english:
Thank you, Llywydd. Today, I'm pleased to announce changes the Welsh Government will make to reflect our manifesto commitments to rebalance the non-domestic rates system, and level the playing field for high-street businesses. We recognise the importance of vibrant retail, hospitality and leisure sectors, and these are central to our ambition to regenerate town centres and to breathe new life into our high streets.

Our work of rebalancing the rates system will be delivered through changes to the existing differential multipliers, improving support for selected hospitality and leisure businesses. An expanded scope for the lower multiplier will be funded by a marginal increase to the higher multiplier, applicable to the highest value properties in the tax base across all sectors.

From 2027-28, selected small to medium-sized hospitality and leisure properties will be subject to the lower multiplier currently applied to retail shops. This will bring eligible hospitality and leisure businesses in line with the permanent support introduced for retailers from this year. Eligible properties with rateable values below £51,000 will attract a 30 per cent reduction in their non-domestic rates bills.

This permanent support will replace and exceed the temporary discretionary relief of 15 per cent for food and drink hospitality properties that is currently being provided. It will mean that a wider range of hospitality and leisure businesses will get the long-term certainty that they need to invest and to grow.

The eligible food and drink hospitality properties are pubs, restaurants, cafes, bars, food courts, licensed clubs and live music venues. The eligible visitor accommodation properties are hotels, guest houses and hostels. And in the leisure sector, the eligible properties are cinemas, theatres, libraries, museums and gyms.

Over 12,500 more properties of the relevant types already attract full relief, and that means that they therefore do not pay any non-domestic rates. There is a balance to strike between the broader support that is provided through the lower multiplier and the resulting impact on the value of the higher multiplier. The higher multiplier will be set at just over 4 per cent above the standard multiplier from 2027-28 onwards. This is a small increase to the existing difference, and it's a fair way to redistribute liability so that we can better support the businesses that are at the heart of our high streets and town centres.

These changes to the differential multipliers are linked with the broader work of the town centres taskforce. This taskforce will take account of national policy frameworks, as well as considering the more tailored support that may be needed in individual town centres. Our approach recognises that needs will vary between places that may be facing different challenges that might go beyond the rate system.

I'll bring forward the regulations required to implement the changes to the differential multipliers in the coming weeks. The regulations will specify the properties that will be subject to the lower multiplier, and amend the value used to calculate the higher multiplier relative to the standard multiplier for any given year. Subject to the approval of this Senedd, the changes will take place on 1 April 2027.

The values of the multipliers for next year will be determined as part of our budget preparations for 2027-28, following the UK Government's autumn budget. I'm proposing to make these changes at the earliest opportunity in this Senedd, to prioritise the improvements that are deliverable and affordable in the short term. The Welsh Government will continue to consider further reforms to the non-domestic rates system that reflect our broader ambitions for Wales. I know that Members across the Chamber are interested in this matter, and ideas for further measures on non-domestic rates will receive a listening ear from me. Diolch.

Well, I'm sure I could have made this statement at any point during the summer term. The statement was ready to be made. I chose in particular to wait for the first day of the Senedd being back in session to make the statement, and I'm making it on the floor of the Senedd in order to receive questions from other parties and from Members here to see how they respond to the statement, and what else they think that this system should deliver. Providing support to those businesses that are, in their broad range, existing in town centres has been a manifesto commitment from Plaid Cymru, and today it is a commitment that we are delivering within Government. I hope that that strikes a chord that will be supported by people across the Senedd who represent communities all across Wales and of all political backgrounds as well.

Thank you for those comments and the welcome and the challenges that you set out there in your contribution. Of course, one of the advantages, hopefully, that the businesses that are eligible for this support will see is that it will be a 30 per cent reduction that will be permanent for them. The reduction that's in place for pubs at the moment is discretionary and is only 15 per cent, and therefore, this will excel compared to that and it will be automatic for those businesses. It will allow those businesses that are eligible to be able to plan on the basis of the guarantee that they will have that, if the regulations on this measure pass, this will be something that they can plan for ahead of time. Of course, we are adding to the system that's already in place for shops, that system that was introduced by the previous finance Minister under the Labour Government, so the use of the multiplier, the different multipliers, was introduced by my predecessor in that context. So what I'm doing is expanding the number of businesses that are eligible for this cut in non-domestic rates.

And it is a first step, as I mentioned, as we start to think about how we can go further with the town centre taskforce that has been set up in terms of developing the high street and supporting the high street as the heart of a number of communities. But also the challenge you set forward is a challenge that is about the system as a whole, of course. You speak particularly about city centres, which have large shops and have important anchor stores in the middle of those cities. It is important, of course, that we think about striking the right balance in terms of supporting the smaller businesses, which is a continuous call coming from Members in this Chamber, but with an eye to not disadvantaging the larger businesses too much. So striking that balance is important. In terms of publishing the exact multipliers that will be operational for 2027, that will have to wait until we have the budget for next year, when that is introduced. That is when that will become operational, will become known. 

And then on the point about the full reform of this system that is needed, I think, as a Senedd—. I hear it from different parties and from different Members: rather than making small changes here and there and sometimes making them in a reactive way, reacting to whatever issue is affecting the economy, we need to look at this area as a whole, in its entirety. I would hope, as we discuss and test out more of the ideas relating to business rates, we will come to a consensus across this Chamber with regard to the political appetite that there is to address this work. I would be happy to be part of that discussion.

On these cliff edges you mentioned—when £51,000 is the limit and if you're one side or the other of that, it's a 30 per cent difference in how much tax you pay—this is one of the considerations certainly that needs to be looked at in the future. So, there are further changes that I think the Government could look into making, with support from this Chamber, and then there is a broader question about addressing and reforming the system as a whole. I'm sure that the discussion on that will continue.

I was obviously too keen to go to the pub to prepare for this statement, so I'll reflect on what everybody has united upon in thinking about the timing of statements. But just very genuinely from me, I could have made this statement during the summer recess, in the peak of the tourism season, but I quite deliberately left it until the first day back. But, yes, I'll consider the timing, and getting back in to the rhythm of the work of this place is something that I need to do.

Yes, just on the issue around a cliff edge, I do recognise that this is a very difficult issue for some businesses who fall the wrong side of a support package of this kind, and only very closely. So, the tapering issue is something that I will be interested in looking at, but I didn't want to delay the simplicity and the ability to make this statement and to move on this level of support of 30 per cent reduction for the hospitality and leisure sectors in this way by trying to do everything at the same time in one go. So, these are issues that I will be returning to, and they are issues, of course, that the high-street taskforce will also want to look at, I'm sure, as are many of the issues that you raise. The issue around whether new start-ups on the high street should be given a holiday period for that first six months to a year of trading as a kind of incentive for them to take up, quite often, empty shops, making local authorities more proactive in their local area to support business growth as well by incentivising growth of businesses and growth of business rate collection, with some payback back to local authorities—. I'm always interested in how we can make these systems include more incentives to do better all the time and to have more economic activity. So, those are some things that I hope the town-centres taskforce will look at, but also that we do in response to the issues that are raised in the Chamber here today and at other times.

On mixed businesses, I've come across this as an issue in my own constituency at different times as well, so I'm aware that it's an issue in the system and a tension. I will need to go back to my officials and see whether there is anything in the greater extent of the categorisation that we're now bringing into the 30 per cent reduction that will enable mixed businesses of the kinds you've described to qualify for this. But I can't give a guarantee on the floor here in any individual case or generally on mixed businesses, but I will look at it to see what is possible.

contributions.text_english: Thank you for your contribution, and thank you for stretching the discussion to other areas that this Senedd will be interested in over the next months and years. As I've said, this is very much a first step to support businesses on our high street. It's a reasonably straightforward support package that we can offer at this time. But there are very many aspects of business rate support that need to be looked at and many ideas here this afternoon. The use of differential multipliers, as you've suggested, is new to the way we do our business rate support in this context. It was first introduced on retail properties and on shops by the predecessor Government; we're extending that today. But we need to, again, think about extending the categorisation and possibly categorising some for the first time, as new businesses and new properties develop within our economy. So, there is much still to do on this. This is a first step. For those businesses that will benefit from this, it is most definitely welcome in very challenging times. But there are an array of different measures that the Government currently works on to support businesses, and there is much that both this Government and the UK Government can do to support businesses in what is a very challenging time.

contributions.item_title_en: 9. Debate: The First Supplementary Budget 2026-27
contributions.text_english:
Llywydd, I move the motion and open the debate on the Welsh Government's first supplementary budget for 2026-27. This supplementary budget is our first opportunity to propose changes to the full budget this year and to start the important process of ensuring that expenditure aligns with our priorities as a new Government. We are focusing, therefore, on a targeted allocation of resources and additional capital. This will enable us to make swift progress on our most important priorities as a Government, while also demonstrating that money is being managed prudently and that there is stability for public services and partners.

Alongside this, as is usual in supplementary budgets, the budget makes formal adaptations to the general level of funds available to Wales in light of the spring statement and the main objectives of the UK Government for this financial year. It also includes a restatement of this year's final budget to reflect the new ministerial portfolios. Moving a first supplementary budget is an early mechanism in the financial year to set out formally changes to the annual budget. The second supplementary budget is the final opportunity to finally formalise the allocations towards the end of a financial year.

This first supplementary budget therefore makes £433 million of additional allocations. This includes £294 million for Welsh Government priorities, and £139 million for budgetary responsibility transfers. The balance of £246 million in unallocated resources and £29,000 in general capital has been held in reserves in the first supplementary budget in order to manage in-year pressures and to respond to priorities. This unallocated funding is our protection against the financial position that we have inherited and against the significant financial pressures that are unfunded within the year, including a total of over £300 million of overspend that the health service is currently reporting. Managing these in-year pressures is a significant challenge, and that challenge is made more difficult because of the tight funding framework that we work within. The unallocated resources funding is there as reserves to be allocated later to help us manage the current pressures in the system, if necessary. We cannot allocate that funding in its entirety so early in the financial year. The previous Government made similar allocations to the NHS in supplementary budgets at the end of the financial year: £200 million in 2025-26, £424 million in 2023-24.

The Welsh Government's settlement is directly linked, as we know, to decisions made by the UK Government. It can change, even in-year, up and down. Only a few days after I appeared before the Finance Committee, the UK Government announced its defence investment plan. That is expected to lead to a direct negative consequence for our capital budget this year. If the cut of 1 per cent anticipated hits all departments of Government equally, that will mean the loss of between £25 million and £30 million immediately during this financial year alone, and there is more to come.

This is a supplementary budget.

It is supplementary to the budget that was presented and passed by the previous Labour Government. It was the deliberate decision of this Government to honour the spending commitments made by the previous Government, not to make changes to funding decisions made by Labour. In that context, I understand what the Conservatives have told me, that not changing the Labour budget makes it impossible for them to vote in favour of this supplementary budget today. I fully understand that.

In addition, our decision too was to start to make some new spending commitments to align with the mandate that we received from the people of Wales through a national election. This budget, therefore, allocates £294 million, which is £164 million in resources and £130 million in capital, to support practical priorities that people can see and feel, as was voted for, such as reducing waiting times in the NHS, expanding funded childcare, ensuring that more pupils receive free school meals, more social homes, supporting transport and crucial maintenance work in our schools and hospitals. In many respects, these were priorities that were seen in the manifestos of other parties during the election period.

Our intention is to invest £145 million in our health system to speed up access to treatment and to improve outcomes for the people of Wales. We are giving priority to providing additional funding to tackle child poverty and to help people across Wales with increasing costs of living, and are allocating an additional £55 million to start to deliver our commitment to transform childcare. This budget also provides £2 million to start to implement the Cynnal pilot scheme. That's an important first step in our broader mission to tackle the terrible scourge of child poverty. We are investing an additional £15 million in free school meals. That will enable us to start to extend provision from September onwards to pupils in secondary schools.

We are also providing £40 million in additional capital to improve the standard of school buildings, and a further capital sum of £5 million will be provided towards the community facilities programme. The first supplementary budget is a routine part of the annual budgetary process. It provides assurances to our public services. It also ensures that members of Senedd committees in their scrutiny work can see clearly the changes to Government decisions in terms of income and expenditure. It's not a surprise to me that a new party to this Senedd, Reform, would question why consequential funding is not merely passed on to the equivalent recipient in Wales, that this Senedd is merely a go-between. It suits their politics to neutralise this institution. But those of us who are pro-devolution, pro-standing up for the independence of this Senedd and our democratic right to make our own choices, I would expect us all to agree that it is for Welsh Ministers in this Senedd to decide how the Welsh budget is spent, and nothing should be presumed for Wales from an allocation happening in England to deal with English matters. For Wales, do not see England. From those early days of Edwina Hart as finance Minister and Rhodri Morgan as First Minister until today, this principle has been upheld by all Welsh Ministers and Governments.

Now, I accept that some of you here who have called for the allocation of extra money related to ALN in England to be allocated to ALN in Wales may still support the right of this Senedd to take its own decisions. But I do say in response to that: beware of blurring these lines and diluting this principle. It's been well defended up until now, by my predecessors and yours.

As a Government, however, we have listened to the genuine calls made by parties in the Senedd, councils and schools to increase the allocation for ALN this year, and have been developing a strategic approach to tackle fundamental challenges, as well as responding to immediate pressures. On the table, in real time, in this Chamber, in this moment is £40 million this financial year of additional funding for additional learning needs, which focuses on activities that are deliverable, including direct funding to schools to stabilise and shore up current provision, and which establishes a coherent national model for local authorities and schools to develop local responses in a consistent way. This allocation will be followed by £40 million next year and the following year to provide some certainty to the sector—a £120 million total package for ALN to ease the pressure on schools and councils and to place ALN on a more sustainable footing for future years.

Passing this supplementary budget today will enable us to have assurance over the allocations to the outlined priorities of £294 million. That will enable us as a Government to carry a smaller risk in committing to allocating £40 million additionally to ALN this year. We will regularise this allocation in our second supplementary budget and include the allocations of £80 million to future annual budgets. If Members vote against or abstain on this budget today and it doesn't pass, the Government will be able to press ahead with the majority of our work and spending on our priorities at our own risk. But, due to the inherited in-year pressures, we will be unable to add to it another risk of £40 million spend. We will then only be able to use the funding allocated by the previous Government in its budget to ALN this year, with no £40 million uplift. However, we will continue to prepare for better future provision for ALN as part of our next year's budget planning.

I ask Members to think carefully, in casting your vote today, of what can be gained and what can be lost. There's £164 million new spend on the NHS, childcare and travel opportunities for your constituents. There's £130 million additional capital money into schools, hospitals and housing. There's a £120 million package for councils and schools for ALN uplift. And to Labour specifically, we offer all of this and your previous Government's budget inherited by Plaid Cymru, its allocations honoured and wholly untouched. This supplementary budget is a good deal for this Senedd and, more importantly, it's a good deal for the people of Wales.

contributions.text_english:
Dirprwy Lywydd, thank you for the opportunity to respond to this debate, as these are such important matters for children, families and schools across Wales. I want to begin by making it clear that this Government has made a commitment to children and young people with additional learning needs. We adopt a strategic approach to make the ALN system sustainable, a system that truly tackles the fundamental challenges rather than responding to short-term pressures.

Our manifesto includes a suite of measures to this end, and the Cabinet Minister for education is already working on priorities for additional learning needs, practical and financial measures. This is a complex matter and it demands a series of complex responses, and that's why the Government has tabled its amendment today.

First of all, I want to deal with the basic assumption that underpins this motion. It suggests that the funding that we receive as a result of decisions made in England should be allocated to the same policy area in Wales. That's not how devolution works. It's Welsh Ministers who are responsible for deciding how funding is earmarked. That's exactly how the previous Welsh Government worked, and that's how this Government will operate too.

Secondly, Dirprwy Lywydd, we must be clear about the nature of this specific consequential funding. The consequential funding received does not reflect new investment to improve services in England. It's funding that the United Kingdom Government has allocated to tackle historical financial deficits that had accumulated in local authorities in England with regard to additional learning needs. In England, therefore, this additional funding is not going towards supporting special educational services, and the consequential is not recurrent. It's one-off funding for this financial year, and the recurrent funding is to arrive in 2028-29.

The Audit Wales report, referred to in our amendment, provides a clear picture of a system that places increasing strain on our local authorities. Local authority expenditure on additional learning needs provision now approaches at least £1 billion per annum. Moreover, according to the report, the system does not have robust arrangements for gathering data, public bodies do not have a full understanding of the costs, and there are major inconsistencies when it comes to provision and fair access. There is a major task ahead for the Government to tackle these multiple deficiencies and to create a far more effective and sustainable system.

contributions.text_english:
As a Government, we recognise and agree with the analysis outlined by Lynne Neagle in introducing this debate. You know better than most, Lynne, of the pressures within our schools and within additional learning needs in contributing to that. We agree that the solution needs to start this financial year, but it does not necessarily need a supplementary budget to start this work; it is already under way, as I said, by the Government Minister. 

It is important at this point, I think, to rehearse again what the resource allocations proposed in this supplementary budget are. It is an addition of £164 million resource only within year, the largest part of which is the £100 million to the NHS to reduce waiting times. Whilst its use will be different to the previous Government's way of tackling waiting lists, it is inherently the same quantum as spent by the previous Labour Government on a waiting list initiative that was brought to an abrupt end just before the election.

The second largest allocation is to childcare: £45 million. Let's break down this £45 million. It is made up of three parts: £18 million to fully fund the commitment made by the previous Government and unfunded in the budget passed on to us; another £7 million is for a workforce rates increase commitment made by the previous Government, but unfunded; and only a £20 million allocation to start the roll-out of Plaid Cymru's additional childcare provision.

Next comes the transport resource allocation of £10 million: £8 million of this to extend the young person's £1 bus fare pilot until the end of March, which was started by the previous Labour Government, with Lib Dem support, and now continued by this Government; then, £2 million is for the north-south bus route—again, a plan started by the previous Government. Indeed, the eight buses for this route were purchased by the previous Government's transport Minister. Plaid Cymru's contribution in this supplementary budget is to allocate resource funding to put drivers in the buses.

The final part of the supplementary budget is a £9 million allocation to priorities primarily identified as Plaid Cymru manifesto commitments: secondary school free school meals; Cynnal, the child poverty payment; and a school swimming programme. This only accounts for £9 million of the £164 million resource allocation.

In voting for this motion today, are Members asking this Government only to reallocate this £9 million to ALN education, or the total of £344 million to ALN, as proposed by Mike Hedges? Or are you saying, as Members, that you do not want us to spend on reducing waiting lists at all, not to spend on childcare commitments made by Labour in Government, not to carry on the £1 bus fare for young people, for where else does the money come from?

And here we come to the crux of this Government's financial position, as inherited from the previous Government. So, yes, when I became finance Minister, I was told that there was a one-off non-recurrent consequential of over £300 million to the Welsh budget as a result of local authority debt write-off in England. But, at the same time, I was told that there were unfunded in-year financial pressures in the budget that I inherited of over £300 million in the NHS and more elsewhere, including childcare, as I have already outlined. So, in one fell swoop, I was both up £300 million and down £300 million. This is why the supplementary budget includes £246 million of unallocated resource to deal with in-year pressures.

Now, careful consideration will be given to the prioritisation of the unallocated funding over the next few months, but it is too early to do so yet, in this first supplementary budget, only two months into this new Government. And things can change over the next months. In fact, they've already changed since my appearance in front of the Finance Committee yesterday morning. Yesterday's UK defence investment plan by the Labour UK Government is to have a negative consequential on our capital budget. Our estimate of a 1 per cent cut in UK Government capital budgets, if it were applied evenly across all UK departments, would lead to a reduction of at least £25 million to £30 million in the Welsh Government's capital budget this financial year, with further similar reductions in future years up to 2029-30. This will cumulatively be significant for the Welsh Government's budget, not miniscule, as some have suggested, with a direct impact on schools, hospitals and transport investment. We also know that the UK Government has indicated there is a further £4.7 billion to be found at the autumn budget. So, this £25 million to £30 million is the minimum cut we can expect to face. It could be cut further within this financial year.

I suspect that the die is already cast on the vote on this motion today. Over my time in this Senedd, I have seen many alliances and coalitions come and go. It seems today that we may well see the birth of a new grand alliance in this Senedd's seventh term: an alliance of right-left-right, a broader church alliance than ever seen before, an alliance forged from political opportunity for some behind me, rather than shared values. I urge all Members to support the Government amendment.

I finish with a genuine offer to interested parties in this Chamber to use this moment, to use this focus on additional learning needs, and to work with us on these benches to design, with local authorities, a sustainable, affordable plan for additional learning needs that provides better outcomes for our young people, and to do so in a long-term, impactful way.

contributions.item_title_en: 5. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Finance: The First Supplementary Budget 2026-27
contributions.text_english:
We have inherited a challenging financial situation, and we face significant pressures across the public sector. This is a supplementary budget—a budget within a financial year. We have therefore chosen to honour the budget voted for in January, a budget that is already in place in our health boards, county councils, national bodies and the voluntary and business sectors. The purpose of this budget is not to destabilise, but to start setting a new direction for public spending in Wales, in line with the priorities the people of Wales voted for in May.

As I mentioned, the financial situation is challenging and the financial pressures within the budgets are significant, especially in the health service. That's why this budget keeps money unallocated to allow us to manage the financial pressures during the year. The consequential funding to the budget from the write-off of local government’s special educational needs debts in England, together with the reserves at the beginning of a financial year, allow this Government to earmark additional funding today while keeping an eye on the ongoing financial pressures that continue within our public sector.

I spoke to the leader of local government in Wales last week to explain that councils will not receive the one-off funding to write off special education debts accumulated by local government in England, as those debts do not exist in Wales in the same way. We of course accept the financial pressure that is on local government and are particularly keen to work with councils and others to plan bespoke special education services that better meet the needs of children and families, whilst also being financially sustainable for the long term. Consequential funding for special educational needs will come into our budget possibly in 2028-29, and unlike this year's one-off funding, that will be recurrent funding. Working closely within the annual budget process will put additional learning needs on a sustainable and affordable footing for the future.

This supplementary budget is not intended to deliver everything, but as a first step towards making sure that our spending plans align with our manifesto. Today, I am confirming £294 million of extra funding: £164 million of resource funding and £130 million of capital funding.

We are prioritising extra money to reduce NHS waiting times. This includes £100 million of resource funding, £25 million of capital funding to develop new surgical and diagnostic hubs across Wales, and £20 million of additional capital for maintenance work in the NHS. This is a total investment of £145 million in our health system to speed up treatment and improve outcomes for the people of Wales. There is no doubt that there is a need for immediate progress on reducing the waiting list backlog, but we must also ensure that we keep waiting times down permanently. This is why we are also reforming the structure of the system, to build long-term capacity.

We have been completely clear that one of our main priorities is to tackle child poverty and support people in Wales with the rising cost of living. An extra £55 million will mean we can make early headway on our commitment to transform childcare. This extra budget will support our intention to accelerate the roll-out of 12 and half hours of childcare per week to all two-year-olds this year.

We are introducing £2 million to begin the implementation of the Cynnal pilot, our child payment of £10 a week for households claiming universal credit. It represents an important first step in our broader mission to tackle the terrible scourge of poverty, which is so damaging to children. 

There is £15 million of extra funding going towards free school meals, as we begin offering free meals to secondary school pupils from families claiming universal credit from September onwards. We will work with schools and local authorities to deliver this. In this budget we are also allocating £40 million of extra capital to improve the quality of our school buildings. Also, an extra £5 million of extra capital will also go to the community facilities programme—an increase of 50 per cent to this year’s budget.

There will be £2 million of resource funding to support the roll-out of the new swimming and water safety programme for schools. This will support our intention to ensure 20 swimming lessons for children in years 4 and 5 in every primary school in Wales. 

There is an extra £8 million in this budget to safeguard £1 bus fares for children and young people. This is a successful scheme that encourages our young people to use buses and reduces their living costs. For decades, public transport in Wales has been insufficient. We will be investing £2 million in a north-south—or south to north—coach service, linking Bangor and Carmarthen, which will be in place from this autumn. This is a scheme that will link communities that were deprived of their rail connection back in the 1960s.

The money that's being announced today is only part of the story. Simply providing additional money, in and of itself, is not a mark of success. How we use that money is just as important. That is why the work that the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution outlined earlier this afternoon about the importance of turning priorities into outcomes goes hand in hand with this supplementary budget, and especially the autumn budget, so that every pound works harder for the people of Wales. 

The financial outlook over the next few years is challenging. It is clear that we need a fairer funding model for Wales. Our aim as a Government is to build a constructive relationship with the UK Government—whoever leads that Government—to argue our case and address the historical underinvestment in Wales.

In my meeting with the Chief Secretary to the Treasury last week, I raised the need for fiscal reform, historical and future rail funding and tackling the industrial legacy of coal tips. We will continue to press for fairness through our engagement with the UK Government, including at the next meeting of the Finance: Interministerial Standing Committee, which will hopefully take place here in Cardiff soon.

contributions.text_english:
The capital allocation available to the Welsh Government, to this Welsh Government, is carried over from a capital allocation that was clearly outlined by Mark Drakeford, my predecessor, as something that he thought, and we agreed, should be allocated by the next Welsh Government. I did reference that in my statement, and it is part of the portfolio of funding that is available to enable this supplementary budget to be made.

I do need to say once more, though, that, in the scrutiny of a budget and in Plaid Cymru's decision to support allocating additional funds to the NHS and to local authorities in January of this year for this financial year, what is available to us as an opposition party is the allocation and the detail of the budget allocation. It is not a deep insight into the financial pressures within Government that that budget could lead to. That's what's new about what Plaid Cymru is seeing and what I've seen as a result of coming into Government. Those pressures are real, they are significant, and that's why this supplementary budget today is not allocating all its revenue or capital, is keeping some of that revenue and capital unallocated in order to meet those pressures and meet any additional issues that will come to pass, possibly, during this year.

The £145 million to the NHS for reducing waiting lists and for capital works as well is something that the people of Wales voted for in voting for a Plaid Cymru Government. It has been advocated by many around this Chamber that this is a priority for so many of us, because they are priorities that our constituents tell us about in our work as their representatives. But this allocation does differ from the allocations that were made by previous Governments. It doesn't just focus on bearing down on those waiting lists. It's not that sticking plaster that Darren Millar referred to earlier, but it does actually start the work also on creating a system that best deals with meeting the pressures that are ongoing, and to stop those waiting lists from increasing year on year, as they have done most recently. You'll have an opportunity, if you choose to, to question the health Minister immediately after this statement.

And yes, on transport, thank you for your welcome for the provisions that we've made for the young person's travel, continuing on the successful scheme that was introduced by the previous Government. And yes, I fully acknowledge that I heard him talk about this scheme often when he was the transport Minister. I was listening to him; he's not listening to me at this point. [Laughter.] I'm going to mention you, Ken, because this is your bus. I'm happy to say that this bus connection between Bangor and Carmarthen was started and developed in your Government with our support as an opposition party. I'm happy for us to call it Bus Ken, if need be, because it is a bus that meets the needs of the communities along the western seaboard that are not met by a rail connection that was taken away.

On ALN, the additional learning needs consequential is provided by the UK Treasury in England to write off historical debts accrued by councils in providing ALN services. It is not money to be used for providing more ALN services in England this year. It is a one-off debt, one-off write-off, so it's not money for service provision. However, as I said earlier, the discussion, the challenge around this consequential has focused our minds as a Government in our early days on the need to work with local authorities and schools to put ALN on a sustainable financial footing. A recurrent consequential for ALN may reach the Welsh block for 2028-29. Therefore, the work to deliver ALN services better for families concerned and more financially sustainable for the authorities delivering the services has already begun. We need to get on top of ALN expenditure. It has grown 2.5 times faster than overall educational spend in the last 10 years, and it is on a trajectory to reach a £1 billion spend within a few years. But this issue is best dealt with on a sustainable, recurrent basis, and properly planned for, and that is the work that I am going to be doing in the context of the annual budget with the Minister for education. We'll work with others, others in this Chamber, to ensure that we find a place where our additional learning needs, and those people who need the services, are better served, equally served throughout Wales, and that it is on a sustainable footing.

contributions.item_title_en: 5. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Finance: The First Supplementary Budget 2026-27
contributions.text_english:
Thank you, Sam Rowlands, and thank you for those questions and comments. This Government is keen to ensure that it is both business friendly and keen to make sure that we support business and economic growth here in Wales. Our top priority for doing that is to establish the national economic development agency in Wales, and we are already in the process of developing that and ensuring that we will have the budgetary requirements for that agency as it needs to come on stream, and those are discussions that I'll continue to have with the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy as we move now to start the annual budget process for establishing next year's annual budget.

There are measures, of course, in this supplementary allocation today that will enable more people to take part in the workplace and contribute to the economy. Our childcare offer is, if not primarily, quite significantly argued for and will see benefit for those people who want to have childcare in order to enable them to either re-enter or re-enter more fully the jobs market. That's an important contribution to our economy. Reducing the travel costs for young people: young people are disincentivised from being able to reach employment opportunities because of significant travel costs, so that in itself as well enables that flexibility within the economic workplace. Tackling child poverty is another priority of this Government. The Cynnal payment and the pilot to establish that is something that we have committed to and we are funding in this supplementary budget. The Minister has established her taskforce to develop the detail of this, and in that detail as well, there will be the need to assess the work that this payment can contribute to, but we do need to be ensuring that more of our children are raised out of poverty.

Thank you for acknowledging the significant £40 million school capital funding allocation. There is no doubt—I've heard it mentioned by many here in the previous Senedd—that the standards of our school buildings are not where our young people or teachers deserve them to be, and so making an inroad and a significant part of the contribution of capital funding here, making an inroad into improving our schools is important.

Moving on, then, to the ALN consequential issue, you do make an important issue around school deficits. We do know that there are deficits that are held by schools, by more schools now than it used to be. The figures that I have show that 27 per cent of schools in Wales have a deficit, and we can also know that some of that deficit is created as a result of the pressures on ALN, but not exclusively ALN; there are other pressures that schools have faced as well. Therefore, these issues are ones that we will want to investigate as we move on now to think about how we ensure that schools are able to budget in a way that enables ALN to be delivered effectively in the school setting and beyond, so that we can get to a place where we are able to have a budgetary position and allocation for ALN, and a service that is planned for in a way that is better value for money, but also meets the needs better of those parents and children that depend on it.

contributions.text_english:
Thank you very much to the former Chair of the Finance Committee. Yes, it was a deliberate decision by this Government to honour the budget passed by the previous Senedd, and to do that because that budget was already operational within our health boards, our local authorities and our voluntary groups who are reliant on Government funding. There are so many different aspects of Welsh public life that will have made plans for expenditure based on the budget passed in January of this year, and therefore that reassurance is provided through the supplementary budget that that budget remains in place for this financial year.

As I've listened to questions and contributions in this Senedd over the past fortnight, I've heard a great deal of criticism that the Government isn't moving swiftly enough and that there are too many plans and too much thought being given to what should be done. Therefore, moving apace is important, but the final point that you make, Peredur, is also important, namely that there have been 27 years of Government that happened before Plaid Cymru came in to fully govern in Wales, and therefore we as Plaid Cymru need to look at all of those layers that have developed within public budgeting in Wales and realign that so that it better reflects what we think are the priorities now for the Welsh Government, namely those that the people of Wales voted for in the election that's just taken place, and those that I think have been requested across many of the parties represented in this Senedd. So, there's a job of work to be done there in terms of the process of developing the budget for the next financial year.

This budget today, this supplementary budget, honours the budget that the previous Government allocated to all public funding in Wales, including ALN. I don't need to point out to you that you were the Minister for education responsible for making the case within the previous budget for an allocation for ALN—greater, if it needed to be, as you've outlined here.

As I've said, we are genuine in our understanding. We know that we need, as a Government, to do more to develop a service that is sustainable and serves the users better than what we've inherited. I don't mean that in an adversarial way. I want to work with people like you, who have the expertise to provide to this Government and across this Chamber, and to the committee that will be established as well, to see that we can get to a place where we have a better system of funding additional learning needs, where it doesn't put the pressure it's putting on the third, as you say, of our schools currently. But I don't want to do that in a way where we are providing a one-off contribution this year that has to end at the end of this year. I want to plan it properly, so that it's done in a way that delivers the best value for both the people who are served by it and for the people who pay taxes in Wales. 

As I said, this is on a trajectory to get to £1 billion in a few years in terms of spend on additional learning needs. If we are going to be spending £1 billion of our Welsh budget on additional learning needs, we need to absolutely make sure that it is spent in the best way. Because at the moment, we still have constituents complaining to us about the service that we have, even though there is two and a half times as much budget spent now on additional learning needs than there would have been three or four years ago. This is growing exponentially, and we need to plan for better delivery on this. I am genuine in wanting to get to that solution. I am not persuaded that the quick fix of this allocation in this year is the way to do that best. I know you have a different view on that. But I do want to ensure that we use this spotlight in this Chamber at this point on additional learning needs to get to a place where we have a better solution on how ALN is funded, how much it needs and how better it can deliver for our young people.

I want to work with people like you, who have the expertise to provide to this Government and across this Chamber, and to the committee that will be established as well, to see that we can get to a place where we have a better system of funding additional learning needs, where it doesn't put the pressure it's putting on the third, as you say, of our schools currently. But I don't want to do that in a way where we are providing a one-off contribution this year that has to end at the end of this year. I want to plan it properly, so that it's done in a way that delivers the best value for both the people who are served by it and for the people who pay taxes in Wales. 

As I said, this is on a trajectory to get to £1 billion in a few years in terms of spend on additional learning needs. If we are going to be spending £1 billion of our Welsh budget on additional learning needs, we need to absolutely make sure that it is spent in the best way. Because at the moment, we still have constituents complaining to us about the service that we have, even though there is two and a half times as much budget spent now on additional learning needs than there would have been three or four years ago. This is growing exponentially, and we need to plan for better delivery on this. I am genuine in wanting to get to that solution. I am not persuaded that the quick fix of this allocation in this year is the way to do that best. I know you have a different view on that. But I do want to ensure that we use this spotlight in this Chamber at this point on additional learning needs to get to a place where we have a better solution on how ALN is funded, how much it needs and how better it can deliver for our young people.

contributions.text_english:
Thank you, and full recognition of your role as a Member in the last Senedd, working collaboratively with the Government to introduce the £1 bus fares for young people. It appears to be a very successful scheme, and that's why this Government has been persuaded to continue with that scheme. In the same way, the recognition from you of that need to look at measures that are going to help the Government and us as a society to tackle child poverty. The work that has started is early work, but it’s work that needs to tackle child poverty. But as you said, there are a number of different elements that will ensure that children are lifted out of child poverty, and it's not just about a direct payment.

You mentioned housing. Of course, there is £20 million of capital funding in this budget for investing in new housing, new social housing. Then, on the point that you made at the end, what does allow us as the Government to be more progressive, to aim even higher in how we use the Welsh pound to deliver services better and to invest more in Wales is, if we have more flexibility in terms of those borrowing powers in particular. The fiscal settlement that we have with the UK Government needs to be reformed.

A great number of powers that are already in place in Scotland aren't available in terms of our budgetary purposes today here. So, the discussion that I started with the Chief Secretary to the Treasury, when I met her, on the need to tackle many of these issues—which aren't huge devolved issues, they are easy to identify and there is specific value in delivering them—will continue with the UK Government. And who knows, maybe the events of the last few days will lead to better outcomes than what we've seen over recent years.

contributions.item_title_en: 5. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Finance: The First Supplementary Budget 2026-27
contributions.text_english:
Thank you for outlining the benefit and the good that will come from the £55 million on extending the childcare provision that's outlined in this supplementary budget. As you've outlined very clearly, childcare costs are a disincentive for people to be in the workplace. We need to have a more vibrant economy in Wales, and in order to enable us to do that we need more people taking part in that economy and contributing to creating wealth.

Childcare is good for the children too—that is something I've heard the Minister talk about often. Multiple studies show that improved access to affordable childcare supports higher employment, particularly among parents and carers, helping more people to enter work and increase their hours. There is a serious job of work that this Government wants to do to make the lives of young families easier, tackle their cost-of-living pressures and enable them to contribute to the economy for the wider public good, as you described it. I'm really pleased that we are able to put additional funding into this and to develop our full childcare policy as we roll that out over the next three years.

contributions.item_title_en: 1. Election of the Presiding Officer under Standing Order 6
contributions.text_english:
Good afternoon and welcome, all, to this Plenary meeting, which is the first meeting of the seventh Senedd. May I start by saying how wonderful it is to see this Chamber full? May I congratulate the 95 of you elected to serve the people of Wales in our national Parliament? The expectations of constituents of us all will be very great, and we have a responsibility to deliver against those expectations, and to do so with dignity, respect and some hwyl too.

As I prepare to leave this role, may I wish you all every success in your important work over the next four years? So, as Llywydd, it's my duty, under Standing Order 6.4, to chair proceedings for the election of a new Presiding Officer. I therefore invite nominations under Standing Order 6.6. Are there any nominations?
contributions.text_original:
Prynhawn da a chroeso, bawb, i'r Cyfarfod Llawn. Hwn yw'r cyfarfod cyntaf o seithfed Senedd Cymru. Gaf i gychwyn drwy ddweud pa mor hyfryd yw hi i weld y Siambr yma yn llawn? Gaf i estyn llongyfarchiadau i'r 95 ohonoch ar gael eich ethol i wasanaethu pobl Cymru yn ein Senedd genedlaethol? Bydd disgwyliadau'r etholwyr yn uchel o bob un ohonom, a'r cyfrifoldeb ar ein hysgwyddau i wireddu'r disgwyliadau hynny, a gwneud hynny gydag urddas, parch a twtsh bach o hwyl hefyd.

Wrth i fi baratoi i adael y swydd yma, gaf i ddymuno pob llwyddiant i chi i gyd yn eich gwaith pwysig dros y pedair blynedd nesaf? Felly, fel Llywydd, fy nyletswydd i o dan Reol Sefydlog 6.4 yw cadeirio'r trafodion ar gyfer ethol Llywydd newydd. Rwy'n gwahodd enwebiadau o dan Reol Sefydlog 6.6. A oes yna Aelod yn cael ei enwebu?

contributions.item_title_en: 1. Election of the Presiding Officer under Standing Order 6
contributions.text_english:
We will now move to the secret ballot, and I will suspend the meeting to conduct that secret ballot. Voting will take place in briefing room 13, which is just outside this Chamber. The ballot will not close until all Members intending to vote have done so.

I have agreed that Sarah Murphy may vote by proxy for reasons of parental leave, and Vikki Howells will exercise the vote on her behalf as a proxy.

The clerk will be responsible for overseeing the voting and the count, and, once the votes cast have been counted from the secret ballot, the bell will be rung so that we may reconvene to announce the result. So, I suspend the meeting.
contributions.text_original:
Byddwn ni nawr yn symud at y bleidlais gyfrinachol, a byddaf i'n atal y cyfarfod, er mwyn hwyluso hynny, dros dro. Bydd y pleidleisio yn digwydd yn ystafell friffio 13, sydd jest y tu allan i'r Siambr yma. Ni fydd y balot yn cau tan fod pob Aelod sy'n bwriadu pleidleisio wedi gwneud hynny.

Rwyf i wedi cytuno y caiff Sarah Murphy bleidleisio drwy ddirprwy am ei bod hi ar absenoldeb rhiant, a bydd Vikki Howells yn bwrw'r bleidlais honno ar ei rhan hi fel dirprwy.

contributions.item_title_en: 1. Election of the Presiding Officer under Standing Order 6
contributions.text_english: We reconvene. I have a result for you following that secret ballot. There were 95 votes cast for Huw Irranca-Davies. In favour there were 85 votes, against nine, and one abstention. There were no spoilt ballot papers. So, I declare, in accordance with Standing Order 6.9, that Huw Irranca-Davies is elected as Presiding Officer of the Senedd. Many congratulations. [Applause.] We will now suspend the meeting for a second or two before the Presiding Officer takes the Chair.
